fields.h1: Hudson Taylor and the Secret of Trusting God for the Impossible
fields.meta_title: Hudson Taylor: The Secret of Trusting God for the Impossible
fields.description: Hudson Taylor took the gospel to inland China with no guaranteed income and staggering obstacles. Here is what his life teaches about faith, dependence, and trusting God for the impossible.
fields.body_html:
By every ordinary calculation, Hudson Taylor should have failed. A young Englishman with poor health and no wealth, he set out to bring the gospel to the vast, closed interior of nineteenth-century China — a land of hundreds of millions who had never heard the name of Christ, hostile to foreigners, with no mission society guaranteeing his support. He founded a mission that trusted God alone for its funds, wore Chinese dress when other missionaries would not, and buried a wife and children in that soil. And against every calculation, God used him to plant the gospel across inland China and to inspire a wave of missions that changed the world. How? The answer is not Taylor’s strength, but the God he learned to trust for the impossible.

Here is what his life teaches about faith, dependence, and trusting God when the task is far bigger than you.

He began where faith always begins: with a God who can

Taylor’s whole life rested on taking Jesus at his word: “All things are possible for one who believes” (Mark 9:23). He did not mean that believing hard enough forces God’s hand, but that a God to whom all things are possible is worth trusting for what looks impossible to us. “Without faith it is impossible to please him,” Scripture says, “for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:6). Taylor staked his life on that reward — not that God would make things easy, but that God would be faithful.

He trusted God for provision — and told no one but God

The most famous feature of Taylor’s mission was its refusal to appeal for money. Like George Müller before him, whom he deeply admired, Taylor made it a principle to tell his needs to God alone and let God move people to give. His conviction rested on a promise: “my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). Time and again, funds arrived exactly when needed, from people who could not have known the need — a lifelong education in the faithfulness of a Father who feeds the birds and clothes the flowers, and who had said, “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Taylor learned that God’s work, done God’s way, would never lack God’s supply.

He was gripped by the need before he was equal to it

Taylor’s mission did not begin with confidence in his own ability; it began with a burden he could not put down. He was haunted by the sheer number of people in inland China dying without ever hearing of Christ — a tide of souls beyond the reach of the few coastal missions. That burden is itself instructive. God’s great works often begin not with the qualified but with the burdened — those who let a need break their hearts and drive them to prayer. Taylor prayed for workers before he had the means to send any, trusting the One who said, “pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers.” And in time God answered, raising up the China Inland Mission and hundreds of workers. The lesson is that you do not wait until you feel equal to a great task before you take up the burden of it; you take up the burden, bring it to God, and let him supply what you lack. Faith for the impossible starts with a heart willing to care about the impossible.

His secret was not effort but abiding

For years Taylor drove himself, striving to be holy and useful in his own strength, and often failing and exhausted. Then a letter from a friend opened to him what he called the exchanged life — the discovery that the Christian’s strength is not his own resolve but Christ’s life within him. He had been trying to hold on to Christ; now he saw that the branch does not strive to cling to the vine but simply rests in its union with it. “I am the vine; you are the branches,” Jesus had said. “Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Taylor traced this out in Union and Communion, and it transformed him: the same man, but now drawing on a strength that was not his own. It is the key to everything else — he could attempt the impossible because the life doing it was Christ’s, not his.

He found God nearest under the greatest pressure

Taylor’s faith was not untested. He buried his beloved wife Maria and several children in China; he suffered illness, opposition, and crushing responsibility. And out of that furnace came the words for which he is most loved:

It doesn’t matter, really, how great the pressure is. It only matters where the pressure lies. See that it never comes between you and the Lord — then, the greater the pressure, the more it presses you to His breast.Hudson Taylor

He had learned what Paul learned: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The pressure that would have driven another man from God only drove Taylor deeper into him. In Separation and Service he pressed on other believers this same secret — that those set apart wholly for God find in him all they need for the service he calls them to.

What his life teaches us

Taylor’s influence outlived him many times over. The China Inland Mission he founded became one of the largest missionary agencies of its age, and the faith principles he modeled — utter dependence on God, identification with the people, trusting God alone for supply — shaped a whole generation of missions that followed. Yet he would have been the first to insist that none of it was his doing. He was a weak and ordinary man who took an extraordinary God at his word, and let God do the rest. That is precisely what makes his life such an encouragement rather than an intimidation: the secret was never Taylor’s greatness but God’s faithfulness, and that same faithfulness is available to every believer.

Most of us will never face Taylor’s particular trials, but every Christian faces some task, need, or fear that is bigger than they are. Taylor’s life hands us a few enduring lessons:

  • Start with God’s ability, not your own. The question is never whether you can, but whether God can — and with him “all things are possible” (Mark 9:23).
  • Take your needs to God and trust him to provide. He has promised to supply every real need (Philippians 4:19); do God’s work in God’s way and you will not lack God’s supply.
  • Draw on Christ’s life, not your willpower. Abide in the Vine (John 15:5). Fruitfulness is the overflow of union with Christ, not the product of strain.
  • Let pressure press you to Christ. Do not let hardship come between you and the Lord; let it drive you into him, where his grace is always sufficient (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Taylor himself insisted he had never made a sacrifice — that whatever he had given up, God had repaid a hundredfold in the joy of knowing and serving him. That is the testimony of a man who trusted God for the impossible and was never once let down. “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13) was not a slogan for Taylor; it was the story of his life. And the God who proved faithful to him is the same God who invites you to trust him with whatever impossible thing you are facing today.

It is worth remembering, too, that Taylor’s faith was ordinary faith, tested and grown over time. He was not born with heroic trust; he built it, decision by decision, on the reliability of God’s promises — often through small experiments in dependence before the large ones. As a young man he practiced trusting God for modest needs, deliberately, so that when the enormous needs of a mission to China came, his faith had muscle. This is a quietly hopeful pattern for the rest of us: faith for the impossible is not a personality trait some are born with and others lack. It is grown, like any trust, by taking God at his word in the small things and watching him prove faithful, until you are ready to trust him in the large. Wherever your faith is today, you can begin where Taylor began — trusting the God who is faithful with the next thing he sets before you, and letting him grow your confidence in him from there. The impossible thing in front of you is not a measure of whether God will act; it is an invitation to watch him act, and to discover, as Taylor did across a lifetime, that the God who cannot fail has never yet abandoned anyone who dared to trust him.
